title: The Recession Alarm Hidden in the Bond Market
subtitle: Bonds are just loans you can trade. Line up their interest rates and you get a curve that has predicted almost every US recession for 50 years.
hook: Stocks get the headlines, but the bond market is bigger and, arguably, smarter. A bond is nothing exotic — it's a loan you can buy and sell. Line up the interest rates on government bonds of different lengths and you get the **yield curve**, and when it does something weird — bends *downward* — economists brace for a recession. It's flagged nearly every US downturn since the 1960s. Today: how a boring loan chart became Wall Street's favorite alarm.

sections.heading: A bond is a tradable loan
sections.body: Buy a government bond and you've lent the government money; it pays you interest (the **yield**) and returns your principal at the end. Because bonds trade, their price moves — and price and yield seesaw: when a bond's price rises, its yield falls, and vice versa. (Why: the future payments are fixed, so paying more for them means earning a smaller return — pure discounting from our earlier lesson.)

sections.heading: The curve, and why it inverts
sections.body: Plot yield against how long until the bond matures — 3 months, 2 years, 10 years — and you get the **yield curve**. Normally it slopes **up**: lock your money away longer, get paid more. But sometimes short-term yields rise *above* long-term ones — the curve **inverts**. That happens when the central bank holds short rates high to fight inflation, while investors, expecting a slowdown (and future rate cuts), pile into long bonds, pushing long yields down. High short + low long = the market betting trouble is coming.

sections.caption: Normal curve slopes up (longer = more yield). Inversion — short above long — is the classic recession warning.

sections.label: A smoke alarm, not a crystal ball
sections.body: The track record is uncanny but not magic: the lag from inversion to recession runs 6–24 months (useless for timing), there've been false-ish alarms, and modern distortions (central-bank bond buying) can bend the curve for non-recession reasons. Treat it as one strong signal among many — impressive, not infallible.

sections.caption: Yield curve inversion — what it is and why markets watch it before recessions.

takeaways: A **bond** is a tradable loan; its **price and yield move in opposite directions**.
The **yield curve** plots yield vs. time-to-maturity; normally it slopes **up**.
**Inversion** (short yields above long) comes from high short rates + investors bracing for a slowdown.
It has preceded almost every US recession since the '60s — with a **6–24 month lag**.
It's a strong signal, not a crystal ball — false alarms and distortions exist.

quiz.q: A bond's price rises. What happens to its yield?
quiz.explain: Fixed future payments + higher price paid = lower return. Price up, yield down.
Inversion = the front end (short) pays more than the long end — the recession warning.

quiz.q: CALLBACK + BOSS: Why does paying MORE for a bond mean earning LESS — and which earlier lesson is that?
options: The bond's future payments are fixed, so a higher price = a smaller return — it's discounting (Day 4), run in reverse
quiz.explain: A bond's price is just the discounted value of its fixed future cash. Pay more today, and the built-in return (yield) is lower. Present value strikes again.

tg_quiz.correct: Right — short above long, the classic alarm.
tg_quiz.wrong: Inversion = short-term yields ABOVE long-term. A recession signal.
tg_quiz.explain: It's flagged almost every US recession since the '60s.
